title: Slot coordination: prefetch vs decode and kernel affinity (draft)
content:
Context
-------
This is a working sketch for a slot-based coordination layer that explicitly separates prefetch (KV warm-up) work from decode token emission, with the goal of improving tail-latency, making micro-batching predictable, and enabling kernel affinity optimizations for locality-sensitive kernels.

Problem statement
-----------------
We see two correlated issues in production workloads:
  * Tail latency spikes when single long-context requests cause KV cache churn while other short requests are waiting on model warm-up.
  * Lockstep prefill-first strategies (block decode until prefill completes) simplify correctness but increase latency for high-priority interactive streams.

Goals
-----
  1. Allow overlap between prefetch/prefill and decode without violating KV consistency or increasing memory pressure unpredictably.
  2. Provide lane-based priority so interactive sessions get timely token emits while background batches handle heavy prefetching.
  3. Use kernel affinity (pinning kernels/streams to lanes) to exploit memory locality and specialized fused kernels (e.g., fused attention for short sequences).
  4. Keep microbatching effective — we still want to amortize per-token kernel overhead.

Design overview (slot-based coordination)
----------------------------------------
We introduce the concept of a "slot": a lightweight scheduling unit representing a logical queue of requests with shared properties. Each slot carries metadata: priority (0..3), expected seq-len distribution, kv-shard-id, and kernel-affinity hints.

Slots are grouped into lanes at runtime:
  * interactive-lane (high priority, low batch-size target)
  * standard-lane (default, medium batch target)
  * background-lane (low priority, large batch target)

Each lane has an associated kernel pool: a set of pre-initialized kernels or CUDA streams tuned for the lane's common sequence-lengths. The scheduler tries to place microbatches on a kernel from the same lane to keep L2/L3 locality and reduce cross-stream synchronization.

Prefetch vs decode phases
-------------------------
We split work per request into phases:
  1) prefetch (walk model layers to warm KV cache for the next N tokens)
  2) speculative early-decode (start scoring/emit for tokens where KV is already available)
  3) final-decode/emit (once fully prefetched or after fallback)

Key behavior: lanes can execute prefetch for background requests opportunistically on spare capacity, while interactive-lane requests may do a minimal prefetch (current token + small horizon) to keep latency low. This avoids blocking interactive flows behind large prefetches.

Microbatching policy
--------------------
Microbatch targets are per-lane: interactive=4, standard=16, background=64 (configurable).
Batches are formed with an adaptive timer: max-wait-ms per lane (interactive=2ms). If a prefetch for a microbatch is not complete by the decode deadline, we allow speculative decoding using partial KV and fall back to re-decode when the rest of the KV arrives (see "speculative decode" below).

KV cache sharding and consistency model
-------------------------------------
We shard the KV cache by model-layer and by slot-assigned kv-shard-id. When a request is scheduled into a slot, it claims a kv-shard mapping for the duration of its prefetch/emit window. This mapping reduces cross-shard evictions.
Consistency rules:
  * Prefetch writes into the per-slot kv-shard buffer; other slots can read only when the buffer reaches layer-consistency markers.
  * Speculative decode can read partially filled shards with documented fallbacks (re-emit/reconciliation).

Kernel affinity and execution pipelines
--------------------------------------
Motivation: certain kernels benefit from data layout and cache hotness. If we can run repeated microbatches of similar sequence-lengths on the same CUDA stream or kernel instance, we reduce kernel warm-up overhead and make fused kernels (short-attention) effective.

Affinity policy:
  * Assign a preferred kernel-class to each lane (e.g., fused-short-attn for interactive, general-attn for background).
  * Maintain an LRU pool of kernel instances per GPU for each kernel-class.
  * When forming a microbatch, pick kernels from the lane pool if available; otherwise fall back to a general kernel.

Speculative decode and reconciliation
-----------------------------------
When partial KV is available we can speculatively decode to reduce perceived latency. Reconciliation options:
  1) best-effort: accept speculative outputs and attach a confidence flag (fast path).
  2) strict: re-decode old tokens once full KV arrives, emit diffs (used only for deterministic endpoints).
  3) hybrid: allow speculative emits for token-by-token streaming, but run a background correctness pass that triggers a rollback only on a high-confidence mismatch.

We prefer hybrid for hosted API streaming: users get low-latency tokens; most times speculative and final agree. Strict mode can be enabled per customer.

Priority lanes and fair-share
----------------------------
High priority lanes preempt background lane prefetchs only at scheduling boundaries (microbatch boundaries) to avoid starvation. Background lanes get guaranteed bandwidth (configurable share). Implemented via token-bucket on work-units per-GPU.

Observability and metrics
------------------------
New metrics to surface:
  * per-lane tail P50/95/99 decode latency
  * fraction of speculative emits vs final-emits
  * kernel-affinity-hit-rate (how often batch used preferred kernel-class)
  * kv-shard-locality (percent of accesses served from same-shard buffer)
  * re-decode-rate (how often reconciliation was needed)

Experimentation plan (A/B)
--------------------------
Phase A (local perf): implement slot-layer assertion tests + synthetic workload (mix of 1s interactive and 512-token batches). Verify that kernel affinity reduces per-token CPU/GPU overhead by >10% on average.
Phase B (staging): enable lanes with conservative defaults, measure P99 reduction and re-decode-rate.
Phase C (canary): route 5% of customer traffic to new scheduler with strict-mode disabled, monitor error/replay window.

Open questions / risks
---------------------
  * Memory accounting complexity: per-slot buffering increases peak working set. Need an eviction policy tuned by lane priority.
  * Re-decode cost: frequent reconciliation can double GPU work for some workloads — need a guardrail threshold.
  * Kernel fragmentation: maintaining many kernel instances per GPU may increase memory usage; we need an LRU with memory soft-limits.
  * Correctness for multi-turn chat: slots must preserve causal KV ordering — careful with speculative cross-slot reads.

Implementation notes (practicalities)
-----------------------------------
  * Scheduler component sits between request-queue and execution engine, emits microbatch descriptors (list of request ids, lane id, kernel-id).
  * Execution engine will expose an "attach-kv-buffer(slot-id)" API so kernels can read per-slot shard layout.
  * Add a lightweight slot-lease mechanism (TTL 250ms) to avoid orphaned buffers.
  * Back-pressure: if a lane exhausts its memory allowance, demote new requests to background-lane or reject with 503 when configured.

Short TODOs
----------
  - [ ] Prototype lane/kernels mapping and measure affinity-hit-rate (PR: see linked_artifacts).
  - [ ] Add metric hooks for speculative emits and re-decode events (metric names above).
  - [ ] Draft cost model: when is speculative decode net-positive vs negative?
  - [ ] Write tests that simulate kv-shard contention and assert no cross-slot leakage.

Notes to reviewers
------------------
This is intentionally a sketch — looking for feedback on:
  * Level of complexity worth adding into the scheduler vs keeping conservative prefill-first semantics.
  * Which reconciliation mode should be the default for hosted API streaming.
  * Practical memory safety knobs you'd want for per-slot buffers.

References and links
--------------------
  - Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/456
  - Slack: #serving-runtime thread (ts in metadata)
  - Jira: SERV-1123 (KV eviction experiments)
